items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: What is the minimum average operating profit an issuer must have over the preceding three years to be eligible to make an initial public offer under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018?
items.answer: At least fifteen crore rupees

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, what percentage of the net offer must an issuer that does not meet the standard eligibility criteria undertake to allot to qualified institutional buyers?
items.answer: At least seventy five per cent.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, what is the minimum percentage of post-issue capital that promoters must hold following a public issue?
items.answer: At least twenty per cent.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, what fraction of the anchor investor portion in a book-built issue is reserved for domestic mutual funds?
items.answer: One-third

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018, for how long is the minimum promoters' contribution in an IPO locked-in where the majority of proceeds are to be used for capital expenditure?
items.answer: Three years from the date of allotment in the initial public offer

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: What is the minimum application value for an entity to qualify as an anchor investor in a public issue on the main board under SEBI ICDR Regulations, 2018?
items.answer: At least ten crore rupees

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under SEBI Takeover Regulations 2011, at what threshold of voting rights does an acquirer become obligated to make a public announcement of an open offer?
items.answer: Twenty-five per cent or more of the voting rights

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under SEBI Takeover Regulations 2011, an acquirer holding 25% or more in a target company may acquire up to what percentage of additional voting rights in a financial year without triggering an open offer obligation?
items.answer: More than five per cent of the voting rights

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
items.question: What is the minimum investment amount an employee or director of the Manager of an Alternative Investment Fund must make in the AIF under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
items.answer: Twenty five lakh rupees

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, what is the maximum permissible gap between two consecutive audit committee meetings?
items.answer: One hundred and twenty days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, a related party transaction is considered material if it exceeds what threshold — Rupees one thousand crore or ten per cent of annual consolidated turnover, whichever is lower?
items.answer: Rupees one thousand crore or ten per cent of the annual consolidated turnover of the listed entity as per the last audited financial statements, whichever is lower

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI PIT Regulations 2015, within how many trading days must a company notify the stock exchange of trades by designated persons after receiving a disclosure?
items.answer: Within two trading days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI PIT Regulations 2015, what is the mandatory cooling-off period that must elapse before trades can commence under an approved trading plan?
items.answer: At least sixty days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Real Estate Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014
items.question: Under SEBI REIT Regulations 2014, what is the minimum asset size required for a REIT to issue units for listing on a recognised stock exchange?
items.answer: Five hundred crore rupees or more

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents) Regulations, 2025
items.question: Under SEBI RTI & STA Regulations 2025, for how long must a registrar to an issue maintain records relating to each issue after its completion?
items.answer: A minimum period of eight years

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations Regulations 2018, what is the maximum shareholding percentage a single entity can hold in a recognised stock exchange without prior written approval of the Board?
items.answer: Five per cent of the paid-up equity share capital

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Under SEBI Credit Rating Agencies Regulations 1999, above what percentage shareholding in an issuer does a credit rating agency become prohibited from rating that issuer's securities?
items.answer: More than ten per cent of the paid-up share capital

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI Depositories and Participants Regulations 2018, what is the threshold shareholding in a depository that triggers the requirement for prior Board approval?
items.answer: More than five per cent of the paid-up equity share capital

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations 2018, what is the minimum total net tangible assets an eligible issuer must have cumulatively demonstrated across all three preceding years (treating each year's minimum separately)?
items.answer: Nine crore rupees (three crore rupees per year × three years)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: If the total portion available for allocation to qualified institutional buyers in a book-built IPO is 900 crore rupees, what is the maximum amount (in crore rupees) that can be allocated to anchor investors who are domestic mutual funds?
items.answer: 180 crore rupees (60% of 900 = 540 crore for anchor investors; one-third of 540 = 180 crore for domestic mutual funds)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: For a listed entity whose audit committee has the minimum permissible number of members under SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, what is the minimum number of those members who must be independent directors?
items.answer: Two independent directors (two-thirds of minimum 3 members = 2, since two-thirds of 3 = 2)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under SEBI Takeover Regulations 2011, if an acquirer pays Rs. 250 per share in an open offer but then buys shares in the open market at Rs. 300 per share within the twenty-six-week post-tendering period, what additional amount per share must be paid to shareholders who accepted the open offer?
items.answer: Rs. 50 per share (Rs. 300 highest price minus Rs. 250 offer price = Rs. 50 difference)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations 2018, if a warrant is allotted on 1 January 2024, what is the latest calendar date on which the warrant holder can exercise the option to acquire equity shares, assuming the warrant exercise price is paid on the last permissible day?
items.answer: 1 October 2025 (warrant tenure ends 18 months from allotment = 1 July 2025; exercise option within 3 months from payment = 1 October 2025)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, if a listed entity holds its first board meeting on 1 April of a financial year, by what latest date must the second board meeting be held?
items.answer: By 29 July of the same year (1 April + 120 days = 29 July)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 (as amended upto 2026)
items.question: Under SEBI Mutual Funds Regulations, an AMC's board has 8 directors. What is the minimum number who must be independent directors?
items.answer: Four independent directors (at least 50% of 8 = 4)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the two passages prescribe different maximum permissible gaps between consecutive meetings for the board and the audit committee respectively?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the two passages impose different shareholding thresholds triggering mandatory Board approval for acquisitions in recognised stock exchanges versus depositories?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, which definition of 'key managerial personnel' is currently in force — the one aligning with Companies Act 2013 sub-section (51) of section 2, or the earlier definition referring to the core management team excluding board members?
items.answer: The definition aligning with Companies Act 2013 sub-section (51) of section 2, effective from 31.01.2023

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Which lock-in regime for minimum promoters' contribution applied before 13 August 2021 — three years or eighteen months?
items.answer: Three years from the date of commencement of commercial production or date of allotment, whichever is later

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI LODR Regulations 2015, which provisions came into force on the date of notification itself rather than after the ninety-day waiting period?
items.answer: Sub-regulation (4) of regulation 23 and regulation 31A

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Was the term 'Delisting Regulations' a defined term in the SEBI Takeover Regulations 2011 at the time those regulations came into force in October 2011?
items.answer: No — the definition of 'Delisting Regulations' was only inserted by the Third Amendment Regulations, 2021, effective from 6 December 2021

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: What was the name of the trading platform for emerging issuers under SEBI ICDR Regulations before 5 April 2019?
items.answer: Institutional trading platform

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Which amendment to SEBI ICDR Regulations broadened the definition of 'associate' to also include entities qualifying as associates under applicable accounting standards?
items.answer: The SEBI (ICDR) (Amendment) Regulations, 2025, effective from 08.03.2025

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Before 7 September 2021, which SEBI regulations were cross-referenced in SEBI LODR Regulations 2015 for the definition of 'non-convertible debt securities'?
items.answer: The SEBI (Issue and Listing of Debt Securities) Regulations, 2008

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Under SEBI ICDR Regulations, where was the draft letter of offer filed before the 2025 amendment?
items.answer: With the Board (SEBI)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: After May 2021, which regulation number in which SEBI regulations defines the term 'main board' for the purposes of SEBI LODR Regulations 2015?
items.answer: Regulation 2(ee) of the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Before September 2018, what phrase was used in the SEBI Takeover Regulations 2011 in the definition of 'frequently traded shares' in place of 'is required to be made under these regulations'?
items.answer: Is made

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992
items.question: The SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations 1992 were enacted under which SEBI Act and year?
items.answer: The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018
items.question: Which was enacted earlier — the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations 2009 or the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations 2018?
items.answer: The SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, 2009 was enacted earlier

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
items.question: In which year was the concept of 'fugitive economic offender' first incorporated into the SEBI LODR Regulations 2015?
items.answer: 2018, effective from 16 November 2018

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Within how many days must a stock exchange forward a completed registration application to SEBI after receiving it?
items.answer: Thirty days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: How does SEBI (Delisting of Equity Shares) Regulations, 2021 define 'compulsory delisting'?
items.answer: Delisting of equity shares of a company by a recognised stock exchange under Chapter V of these regulations.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the two passages together indicate that open-market buy-back through stock exchanges is permitted under SEBI (Buy-Back of Securities) Regulations 2018?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Describe the step-by-step reduction in the maximum open-market buy-back limit through stock exchanges under SEBI Regulations, from 2023 to the final prohibition.
items.answer: 15% (until March 31, 2023) → 10% (until March 31, 2024) → 5% (until March 31, 2025) → Complete prohibition from April 1, 2025.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: A company completed its buy-back (i.e., made the final payment to shareholders) on June 15, 2025. What is the earliest date on which it can launch its next buy-back offer?
items.answer: June 15, 2026 — one year from the expiry date (June 15, 2025) of the buyback period of the preceding offer.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014
items.question: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, what is the combined monetary cap on permissible pecuniary relationships with the InvIT for a person to qualify as an independent director of the investment manager?
items.answer: Two per cent of its gross turnover or total income, or fifty lakh rupees, whichever is lower

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue and Listing of Municipal Debt Securities) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI (Issue and Listing of Municipal Debt Securities) Regulations 2015, within how many days of the relevant trigger date may SEBI specify changes or issue observations on a draft offer document?
items.answer: Twenty one days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Issue and Listing of Municipal Debt Securities) Regulations, 2015
items.question: Under SEBI (Issue and Listing of Municipal Debt Securities) Regulations 2015, for how many days must the draft offer document be publicly available on the designated stock exchange's website for public comments?
items.answer: Fifteen days

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014
items.question: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, if an entity associated with the InvIT has a gross turnover of ten crore rupees, what is the maximum permissible pecuniary relationship an independent director candidate may have with it â€” applying the two per cent cap or the fifty lakh rupee cap?
items.answer: Twenty lakh rupees (two per cent of ten crore rupees, being lower than fifty lakh rupees â€” the rule applies whichever is lower)

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Infrastructure Investment Trusts) Regulations, 2014
items.question: Under SEBI (InvIT) Regulations 2014, a consulting firm had transactions worth eight lakh rupees with the InvIT in FY2023, and its gross turnover for that year was ninety lakh rupees. Would a partner of that firm be disqualified from acting as an independent director of the investment manager for FY2026?
items.answer: No. Eight lakh rupees out of ninety lakh rupees is approximately 8.9 per cent, which is below the ten per cent threshold; the disqualification criterion is not triggered

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: What minimum proportion of the board of directors of an AMC must comprise directors who are not associated with the sponsor, its subsidiaries, or the trustees?
items.answer: At least fifty per cent

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: What restriction does SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996 impose on the Chairman of an asset management company?
items.answer: The Chairman of the asset management company is not a trustee of any mutual fund

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: What is the minimum proportion of independent persons required among the trustees of a mutual fund under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996?
items.answer: Two-thirds

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: Under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, are directors, officers or employees of an AMC eligible to be appointed as trustees of any mutual fund?
items.answer: No. No asset management company and no director (including independent director), officer or employee of an asset management company shall be eligible to be appointed as a trustee of any mutual fund.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: What requirement applies to the Chairperson of a trustee company appointed as trustee of a mutual fund under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996?
items.answer: The Chairperson of the board of directors of the trustee company shall be an independent director

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: What board composition requirement must an AMC meet after its sponsor disassociates from the mutual fund?
items.answer: The board of directors shall have at least two third independent directors

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: Under the Seventh Schedule of SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, what is the standard investment limit for debt instruments issued by a single issuer, and under what approval can it be extended to 12% of NAV?
items.answer: 10% of NAV; may be extended to 12% with prior approval of both the Board of Trustees and the Board of Directors of the AMC

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: On what price basis must inter-scheme transfers of quoted securities between schemes of the same mutual fund be conducted?
items.answer: At the prevailing market price for quoted instruments on spot basis

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: Under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, whose prior approval is required before a director of an AMC can be appointed?
items.answer: Prior approval of the trustees

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: Within what period must an AMC file detailed bio-data of a newly appointed director with the trustees and the Board?
items.answer: Within fifteen days of their appointment

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: To what maximum percentage of NAV can the single-issuer debt investment limit be extended, and whose approvals are needed for this extension?
items.answer: Up to 12% of NAV, with prior approval of both the Board of Trustees and the Board of Directors of the AMC

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996
items.question: Under the original SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, were mutual fund schemes permitted to use scheme funds in option trading, short selling, or carry forward transactions?
items.answer: No. The original Regulation 45 absolutely prohibited the use of scheme funds in option trading, short selling, or carry forward transactions.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
items.question: What is the minimum investment that an investor must make in an Alternative Investment Fund scheme under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012? Are there any exceptions to this minimum?
items.answer: Under Regulation 10(c), the minimum investment by any investor in an AIF scheme is Rs one crore. Two exceptions apply: (1) employees or directors of the AIF, or employees or directors of the Manager, have a reduced minimum of Rs twenty-five lakh; (2) the minimum investment requirement does not apply at all to accredited investors.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
items.question: What are the conditions under which the units of a close-ended AIF may be listed on a stock exchange under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
items.answer: Under Regulation 14, units of a close-ended AIF may be listed on a stock exchange subject to two conditions: (1) the minimum tradable lot must be Rs one crore; and (2) listing is permitted only after the final close of the fund or scheme. Listing is not permitted prior to the final close.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds) Regulations, 2012
items.question: A Category II AIF has 4 investors: an external institutional investor, a director of the Manager, an employee of the AIF, and an accredited investor. Their proposed investments are Rs 75 lakh, Rs 20 lakh, Rs 30 lakh, and Rs 50 lakh respectively. Which investments, if any, fail to meet the minimum investment requirements under SEBI AIF Regulations, 2012?
items.answer: External institutional investor (Rs 75 lakh): fails the minimum of Rs 1 crore. Director of the Manager (Rs 20 lakh): fails the reduced minimum of Rs 25 lakh applicable to manager's directors. Employee of AIF (Rs 30 lakh): meets the Rs 25 lakh minimum for AIF employees. Accredited investor (Rs 50 lakh): no minimum applies — Regulation 10(c) does not apply to accredited investors. Therefore, two investments fail: the external institutional investor (Rs 75 lakh < Rs 1 crore) and the director of the Manager (Rs 20 lakh < Rs 25 lakh).

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Who are the eligible categories of promoters for a credit rating agency under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 4, a credit rating agency must be promoted by one of the following: (a) a public financial institution; (b) a scheduled commercial bank in the RBI's second schedule; (c) a foreign bank operating in India with RBI approval; (d) a foreign CRA incorporated in a FATF member jurisdiction, recognised under their law, with at least five years' experience in rating securities; or (e) any company or body corporate with a continuous net worth of at least Rs 100 crore per audited accounts for the previous five years.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What are the minimum eligibility criteria relating to corporate form, business objects, and net worth for a credit rating agency applicant under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 5, a CRA applicant must satisfy three minimum requirements: (a) it must be set up and registered as a company under the Companies Act, 2013; (b) its Memorandum of Association must specify rating activity as one of its main objects; and (c) it must have a minimum net worth of Rs twenty-five crore.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: How long is a certificate of registration granted to a credit rating agency under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 valid?
items.answer: Under Regulation 8(2), the certificate of registration is valid unless it is suspended or cancelled by the Board — it has no fixed expiry date.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What ongoing net worth requirement must a credit rating agency maintain at all times under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? What transitional relief was provided for existing CRAs?
items.answer: Under Regulation 9(d), a credit rating agency must at all times maintain a minimum net worth of Rs twenty-five crore. Existing CRAs that were already registered and had a net worth below Rs twenty-five crore at the time of the 2018 amendment were given transitional relief — they must increase their net worth to the Rs 25 crore minimum within three years from the date of notification of the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What shareholding requirement must the promoter of a credit rating agency maintain under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, and for how long?
items.answer: Under Regulation 9(e), the promoter of a credit rating agency must maintain a minimum shareholding of 26% in the credit rating agency for a minimum period of three years from the date of grant of registration by the Board.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What restrictions apply to the activities a credit rating agency may undertake under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 9(f), a CRA shall not carry out any activity other than the rating of securities that are listed or proposed to be listed on a stock exchange recognized by SEBI. Two exceptions apply: (1) the CRA may carry out any other activity as may be specified by the Board; and (2) the CRA may carry out rating of financial instruments under the purview of any other financial sector regulator or authority as specified by the Board.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What must a written agreement between a credit rating agency and its client contain under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 14, the written agreement must include: (a) the rights and liabilities of each party; (b) the fee to be charged; (c) an obligation on the client to co-operate for periodic review of the rating during the tenure of the rated instrument; (d) an obligation on the client to provide true, adequate, and timely information; (e) an obligation on the CRA to disclose the rating assigned to the client's securities through regular methods of dissemination, even if the rating is not accepted by the client; and (f) an obligation on the client to disclose in the offer document all ratings assigned in the last three years and any ratings by other CRAs not accepted by the client.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: How must a credit rating agency disseminate information about newly assigned ratings and rating changes under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? What additional step is required for listed company securities?
items.answer: Under Regulation 15(2), a CRA must promptly disseminate information about newly assigned ratings and changes in earlier ratings through press releases and websites. For securities issued by listed companies, the information must additionally be provided simultaneously to the concerned regional stock exchange and to all stock exchanges where the securities are listed.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What must a credit rating agency do if a client fails to cooperate during the rating review process under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Can a CRA withdraw a rating while the security's obligations are outstanding?
items.answer: Under Regulation 16(2), if a client fails to cooperate, the CRA must still carry out the review on the basis of best available information (or as specified by the Board), and must disclose to investors that the rating is based on best available information due to lack of client cooperation. Under Regulation 16(3), a CRA may not withdraw a rating so long as the obligations under the rated security are outstanding — withdrawal is only permitted if the rated company is wound up, or merged/amalgamated with another company (or as otherwise specified by the Board).

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What disclosure obligations about rating definitions and rationale must a credit rating agency comply with under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 18, a CRA must: (1) make public the definitions of the concerned rating with the symbol, and must state that ratings do not constitute recommendations to buy, hold, or sell any securities; and (2) make available to the general public information on the rationale of its ratings, which must cover both factors justifying a favourable assessment and factors constituting a risk.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: For how long and what types of records must a credit rating agency maintain under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 21(1), a CRA must maintain all records for a minimum period of five years. The required records include: balance sheets, profit and loss accounts, auditor's reports, client agreements, information and correspondence from clients, ratings assigned (including upgrades and downgrades), rating notes and committee decisions, rating assignment letters, and fee particulars.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Within what time period must a credit rating agency rectify deficiencies identified in the auditor's report under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 22, a credit rating agency must take steps to rectify any deficiencies identified in the auditor's report (insofar as they relate to the rating of securities activity) within two months from the date of the auditor's report.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Who has the authority to take rating decisions (including rating changes) under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Can a CRA rate its own securities?
items.answer: Under Regulation 24(4), all rating decisions — including decisions on changes in rating — must be taken by the rating committee. Individual analysts or management cannot unilaterally assign or change ratings. Under Regulation 24(8), a CRA is explicitly prohibited from rating securities issued by itself.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What shareholding restrictions apply between credit rating agencies under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999? Are there any exemptions?
items.answer: Under Regulation 24A, a CRA may not directly or indirectly hold 10% or more shareholding or voting rights in any other CRA, and may not have board representation in any other CRA. Additionally, any shareholder holding 10% or more in one CRA may not hold 10% or more (directly or indirectly) in any other CRA. There is an exemption: these cross-shareholding restrictions do not apply to holdings by Pension Funds, Insurance Schemes, and Mutual Fund Schemes.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, can a credit rating agency rate the securities of its own promoter? What additional restriction applies when the promoter is a lending institution?
items.answer: No. Under Regulation 26(1), a CRA is prohibited from rating any security issued by its promoter. Under Regulation 26(2), if the promoter is a lending institution, there is an additional structural restriction — no Chairman, director, or employee of the lending institution-promoter may simultaneously be a Chairman, director, or employee of the credit rating agency or its rating committee.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What conflict-of-interest restrictions apply to the rating of securities of promoter-connected entities under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 27(1), a CRA shall not rate securities of: (a) a borrower of its promoter; (b) a subsidiary of its promoter; or (c) an associate of its promoter — if there are common Chairmen, directors, or employees between the CRA and such entities, or common persons on the rating committee. Under Regulation 27(2), a CRA shall also not rate securities of its own associate or subsidiary if the CRA or its rating committee shares a Chairman, director, or employee with such entities.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 (as amended), can an entity provide ESG ratings without registration? What transitional period was provided to existing ESG rating providers?
items.answer: No. Under Regulation 28C, no person may act as an ESG rating provider without obtaining a certificate from the Board. Existing ESG rating providers operating before the regulation came into force were provided a transitional period of six months (or such other period as specified by the Board) to continue operations. If they filed an application for registration within the six-month period, they could continue until the disposal of their application.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What are the ongoing and application-time liquid net worth requirements for a Category I ESG rating provider under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: Under Regulation 28E(m)(iv), a Category I ESG rating provider must maintain a minimum liquid net worth of Rs 5 crore at all times on an ongoing basis. At the time of making the application for registration, the applicant must have a minimum liquid net worth equal to the higher of: (A) Rs 10 crore, or (B) Rs 5 crore plus the applicant's own projected target of cumulative cash losses until its targeted breakeven date.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A credit rating agency registered with SEBI had a net worth of Rs 18 crore at the time the 2018 Amendment Regulations were notified. By how much must it increase its net worth to comply with the requirement, and by when?
items.answer: The minimum required net worth is Rs 25 crore. The CRA's current net worth is Rs 18 crore. Required increase = Rs 25 crore − Rs 18 crore = Rs 7 crore. The CRA must increase its net worth by Rs 7 crore within three years from the date of notification of the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A foreign credit rating agency was incorporated in its home country in January 2018 and began actively rating securities in its home jurisdiction from July 2019. It applies to promote a new CRA in India in December 2025. Does it meet the 'minimum of five years' experience in rating securities' requirement under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: The foreign CRA began rating securities from July 2019. By December 2025, it has had 6 years and 5 months of rating experience (July 2019 to December 2025). This exceeds the minimum five-year experience requirement. Yes, the foreign CRA meets the five-year experience requirement.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: An auditor submits a report to a CRA on October 3, 2025, identifying deficiencies in its rating activities. What is the deadline by which the CRA must take steps to rectify these deficiencies under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: The CRA must take steps to rectify the deficiencies within two months from the date of the auditor's report. Date of report: October 3, 2025. Adding two months: December 3, 2025. The deadline for rectification is December 3, 2025.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A CRA's promoter holds 35% of the CRA's shares at the time of registration. The CRA was granted registration on April 1, 2023. Can the promoter legally reduce its shareholding to 20% on June 15, 2026?
items.answer: The promoter must maintain at least 26% shareholding for a minimum of three years from the date of grant of registration. Three years from April 1, 2023 = April 1, 2026. June 15, 2026 is after April 1, 2026, so the lock-in period of three years has expired by then. After April 1, 2026, the promoter is no longer bound by the 3-year lock-in. However, reducing to 20% would breach the minimum 26% threshold if this obligation is ongoing beyond the three-year period (which the regulation's wording 'for a minimum period of three years' suggests is a lock-in, not a permanent requirement). The regulation specifies a minimum period of three years; after that, the 26% floor from Regulation 9(e) no longer applies as a mandatory minimum. Therefore, the promoter can reduce its shareholding to 20% on June 15, 2026.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A Category I ESG rating provider applicant projects cumulative cash losses of Rs 6 crore until breakeven. What is the minimum liquid net worth the applicant must demonstrate at the time of filing the registration application?
items.answer: The minimum liquid net worth at application time is the higher of: (A) Rs 10 crore, or (B) Rs 5 crore + projected cumulative cash losses until breakeven = Rs 5 crore + Rs 6 crore = Rs 11 crore. Since Rs 11 crore > Rs 10 crore, the minimum required liquid net worth at application time is Rs 11 crore.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A Category II ESG rating provider applicant projects cumulative cash losses of Rs 8 lakh until breakeven. What is the minimum liquid net worth at application time, and how does it compare to the ongoing maintenance requirement?
items.answer: At application time, the minimum is the higher of: (A) Rs 20 lakh, or (B) Rs 10 lakh + Rs 8 lakh (projected losses) = Rs 18 lakh. Since Rs 20 lakh > Rs 18 lakh, the minimum liquid net worth at application time is Rs 20 lakh. The ongoing maintenance requirement is Rs 10 lakh. Therefore, the application-time requirement (Rs 20 lakh) is double the ongoing maintenance requirement (Rs 10 lakh).

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Institution X holds 12% of the shares of CRA-1. It proposes to acquire a 9% stake in CRA-2. Would this acquisition violate Regulation 24A(2) of the SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: No, the proposed acquisition would not violate Regulation 24A(2). The restriction applies to a shareholder holding 10% or more in one CRA acquiring 10% or more in another CRA. Institution X already holds 12% (≥10%) in CRA-1. However, the proposed acquisition in CRA-2 is only 9%, which is below the 10% threshold. Since the combined holding in CRA-2 (9%) is less than 10%, the restriction under Regulation 24A(2) is not triggered. The acquisition is permissible.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: A body corporate files an application to promote a credit rating agency in December 2025. Its audited net worth for the preceding years was: 2020-21: Rs 95 crore; 2021-22: Rs 102 crore; 2022-23: Rs 110 crore; 2023-24: Rs 108 crore; 2024-25: Rs 115 crore. Does it meet the Regulation 4(e) promoter eligibility criterion?
items.answer: The requirement under Regulation 4(e) is a continuous net worth of at least Rs 100 crore per audited annual accounts for the previous five years. The five years preceding December 2025 would be FY 2020-21 through FY 2024-25. Net worth history: FY 2020-21: Rs 95 crore (fails — below Rs 100 crore), FY 2021-22: Rs 102 crore, FY 2022-23: Rs 110 crore, FY 2023-24: Rs 108 crore, FY 2024-25: Rs 115 crore. Since FY 2020-21 (Rs 95 crore) is below the Rs 100 crore threshold, the 'continuous' net worth requirement is not met. The body corporate does not meet the eligibility criterion under Regulation 4(e).

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do these two versions of Regulation 8(2) impose the same validity period for a credit rating agency's certificate of registration?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the original and 2018-amended versions of Regulation 5(c) prescribe the same minimum net worth requirement for credit rating agency applicants?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the original and 2018-amended versions of Regulation 9(f) define the same permissible scope of rating activities for a credit rating agency?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the original and 2018-amended versions of Regulation 16(3) provide the same grounds for a credit rating agency to withdraw a rating of an outstanding security?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the original and 2021-amended definitions of 'credit rating agency' under Regulation 2(h) cover the same scope of rating activity?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: When was the minimum net worth requirement for credit rating agency applicants under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 raised, and by how much was it increased?
items.answer: The minimum net worth requirement was raised by the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018, with effect from 30 May 2018. The original 1999 regulations set a minimum of Rs five crore. The 2018 amendment increased this to Rs twenty-five crore — a five-fold increase of Rs twenty crore.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Under the original SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999, what was the mandatory dual-rating requirement for large debt issues, and when was it removed?
items.answer: Under the original Regulation 14(g), a client was required to obtain ratings from at least two different credit rating agencies for any debt securities issue of Rs 100 crore or more. This mandatory dual-rating requirement was removed by the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2011, with effect from 27 December 2011. The 2011 amendment replaced this specific dual-rating obligation with a general requirement to obtain a rating 'in accordance with the relevant regulations.'

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: Describe the evolution of the certificate validity regime for credit rating agencies under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 from the original regulations through to the current position.
items.answer: The evolution of certificate validity for CRAs under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 went through three stages: (1) Original (1999): The original regulation prescribed a fixed validity period of three years for the certificate of registration. (2) 2011 Amendment (w.e.f. 05-07-2011): SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2011 introduced a two-stage regime — an 'initial registration' valid for five years, after which the CRA could apply for 'permanent registration' (application to be made three months before expiry of the initial certificate). (3) 2016 Amendment (w.e.f. 08-12-2016): The SEBI (Change in Conditions of Registration of Certain Intermediaries) (Amendment) Regulations, 2016 abolished both the initial/permanent registration distinction and all fixed validity periods — the certificate is now valid in perpetuity unless suspended or cancelled by SEBI.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What change did the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 make to the definition of 'credit rating agency' under Regulation 2(h)?
items.answer: The SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2021 (w.e.f. 03-08-2021) substituted the definition of 'credit rating agency' under Regulation 2(h). The original definition restricted 'credit rating agencies' to entities rating securities 'offered by way of public or rights issue' — covering only primary market issuances. The 2021 amendment broadened the definition to cover rating of securities 'that are listed or proposed to be listed on a stock exchange recognized by the Board' — expanding the scope to include all listed securities and not just those offered via public or rights issues.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: When was the regulatory framework for ESG rating providers introduced under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: The regulatory framework for ESG rating providers was introduced through the insertion of Chapter IVA (comprising Regulations 28A to 28I) by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2023, with effect from 4 July 2023. Prior to this amendment, SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 contained no provisions specifically governing ESG rating providers.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: When was the 26% minimum promoter shareholding requirement for credit rating agencies introduced under SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: The requirement for a minimum promoter shareholding of 26% in a credit rating agency was introduced by the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018, with effect from 30 May 2018. Prior to this amendment, the SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 did not prescribe any minimum shareholding requirement for promoters. The 2018 amendment inserted Regulation 5(l) (eligibility criterion) and Regulation 9(e) (ongoing condition of certificate) to impose this requirement.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: When were the cross-shareholding restrictions between credit rating agencies first introduced in SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999?
items.answer: The cross-shareholding restrictions between credit rating agencies (Regulation 24A) were first introduced by the SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018, with effect from 30 May 2018. Prior to the 2018 amendment, the SEBI (CRA) Regulations, 1999 did not contain any specific prohibition on CRAs holding shares in other CRAs or shareholders of one CRA holding 10% or more in another CRA.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) Regulations, 1999
items.question: What change did the SEBI (CRA) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 make to the continuous monitoring obligation under Regulation 15(1)?
items.answer: The SEBI (Credit Rating Agencies) (Amendment) Regulations, 2018 (w.e.f. 30-05-2018) added a qualifying carveout to the continuous monitoring obligation in Regulation 15(1). The original version required CRAs to continuously monitor ratings 'during the lifetime of securities rated by it' with no exception. The 2018 amendment added the phrase 'unless the rating is withdrawn, subject to the provisions of regulation 16(3)' — clarifying that the monitoring obligation ceases if and when a rating is legitimately withdrawn in accordance with the conditions specified in Regulation 16(3) (i.e., winding up, merger, or as specified by the Board).

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 3(1) of SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations 2011, what voting rights threshold triggers the mandatory open offer obligation?
items.answer: 25% or more of the voting rights in the target company (when combined with shares held by the acquirer and persons acting in concert).

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer holds 30% voting rights in a target company. What is the maximum additional percentage of voting rights they can acquire in a single financial year under Regulation 3(2) without triggering an open offer?
items.answer: 5% of voting rights per financial year.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Can an acquirer acquire control over a target company without making a public announcement of an open offer, even if they do not acquire any new shares?
items.answer: No. Regulation 4 states that irrespective of acquisition or holding of shares or voting rights, no acquirer shall acquire control over a target company without making a public announcement of an open offer.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 5(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, under what condition is an indirect acquisition treated as a direct acquisition for all purposes of the regulations?
items.answer: When the proportionate NAV, proportionate sales turnover, or proportionate market capitalisation of the target company exceeds 80% of the consolidated NAV, consolidated sales turnover, or enterprise value (respectively) of the entity being acquired, on the basis of the most recent audited annual financial statements.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What shareholding range qualifies an acquirer to voluntarily make a public announcement of an open offer under Regulation 6(1) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
items.answer: The acquirer must hold shares or voting rights of 25% or more but less than the maximum permissible non-public shareholding, and the aggregate shareholding after completion of the offer must not exceed the maximum permissible non-public shareholding.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 6(2), after completing a voluntary open offer, for how long is the acquirer prohibited from acquiring further shares of the target company (other than through another voluntary open offer)?
items.answer: Six months after completion of the open offer.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What does Regulation 6A of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 prohibit, and what exception does it carve out for wilful defaulters?
items.answer: Regulation 6A prohibits wilful defaulters from making a public announcement of an open offer or entering into any transaction triggering an open offer obligation. However, it does not prohibit a wilful defaulter from making a competing offer when another person has made an open offer for shares of the same target company.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 7(1) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, what is the minimum open offer size for a mandatory open offer triggered under Regulations 3 or 4?
items.answer: At least 26% of the total shares of the target company (as of the tenth working day from the closure of the tendering period).

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What happens to the offer price if an acquirer purchases shares of the target company during the offer period at a price higher than the declared offer price under Regulation 8(8)?
items.answer: The offer price automatically stands revised to the highest price paid or payable for such acquisition. However, no such acquisition is permitted after the third working day prior to the commencement of the tendering period and during the tendering period.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 8(10), if an acquirer buys shares of the target company within 26 weeks after the tendering period at a price higher than the offer price, what obligation arises and within what timeframe must it be fulfilled?
items.answer: The acquirer must pay the difference between the highest acquisition price and the open offer price to all shareholders whose shares were accepted in the open offer, within 60 days from the date of such acquisition. The obligation does not apply to acquisitions under another open offer, the Delisting Regulations, or ordinary open market purchases not involving negotiated transactions.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What conditions must listed shares offered as non-cash consideration in an open offer satisfy under Regulation 9(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
items.answer: The shares must: (a) be listed and frequently traded; (b) have been listed for at least 2 years before the date of public announcement; (c) the issuer must have redressed at least 95% of investor complaints in the preceding calendar quarter; (d) the issuer must have materially complied with listing regulations for at least 2 years preceding the public announcement; (e) impact of auditors' qualifications must not exceed 5% of net profit or loss after tax for three preceding financial years; and (f) SEBI must not have issued any direction restricting the issuer's access to capital markets or issuance of fresh shares.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 10(3), what must a shareholder do to claim exemption from making an open offer when their voting rights exceed the threshold solely because of a buy-back by the target company?
items.answer: The shareholder must reduce their shareholding such that voting rights fall below the 25% threshold within 90 days from the date of closure of the buy-back offer.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What is the key independence requirement for the manager to the open offer under Regulation 12(1) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
items.answer: The manager to the open offer must be a SEBI-registered merchant banker who is not an associate of the acquirer.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 16(4) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, within how many working days must SEBI give its comments on the draft letter of offer, and what is the consequence if no comments are given within that period?
items.answer: SEBI must give its comments within 15 working days of receipt of the draft letter of offer. If no comments are issued within this period, it is deemed that SEBI does not have comments to offer. If SEBI seeks clarifications, the deadline extends to the fifth working day from receipt of a satisfactory reply.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 17(10)(e), if an acquirer's escrow account is forfeited for non-fulfillment of open offer obligations, how is the forfeited amount distributed?
items.answer: After deduction of expenses of registered market intermediaries: one-third to the target company; one-third to the Investor Protection and Education Fund (IPEF); and one-third distributed pro-rata among shareholders who accepted the open offer.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under what condition and after what period may an acquirer complete the underlying acquisition before the expiry of the offer period under Regulation 22(2)?
items.answer: The acquirer may complete the acquisition after expiry of 21 working days from the date of the detailed public statement, provided they have deposited in the escrow account, in cash, an amount equal to the entire consideration payable under the open offer assuming full acceptance.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Chapter V (Disclosure provisions) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, when must a disclosure of acquisition be made if the acquisition aggregates to 5% or more, and within what timeframe must the disclosure be filed?
items.answer: An acquirer whose aggregate acquisition reaches 5% or more must disclose their aggregate shareholding and voting rights. Additionally, any person already holding 5% or more must disclose any change in shareholding exceeding 2%. All such disclosures must be made within two working days of the acquisition or disposal to every stock exchange where the target company is listed and to the target company at its registered office.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: Under Regulation 26(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, what actions is the target company's board of directors prohibited from taking during the offer period without shareholder approval by postal ballot?
items.answer: The board is prohibited from: (a) alienating material assets outside ordinary course of business; (b) effecting material borrowings outside ordinary course; (c) issuing unissued securities with voting rights; (d) implementing share buy-backs or changing capital structure; (e) entering into, amending or terminating material contracts outside ordinary course; and (f) accelerating any contingent vesting of rights such as ESOPs.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer makes a mandatory open offer where the total consideration payable is Rs 1,200 crore. What is the minimum escrow amount they must create under Regulation 17(1) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
items.answer: Rs 125 crore (25% of first Rs 500 crore) + Rs 70 crore (10% of balance Rs 700 crore) = Rs 195 crore.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer holds 28% voting rights in a listed company with 10 crore total shares outstanding. What is the maximum number of additional shares they can acquire in financial year 2024-25 without triggering a mandatory open offer under Regulation 3(2)?
items.answer: 5% of 10 crore = 50 lakh shares.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: A listed company has 50 crore shares outstanding. An acquirer acquires shares triggering a mandatory open offer under Regulation 3(1). What is the minimum number of shares for which the open offer must be made under Regulation 7(1)?
items.answer: 26% of 50 crore = 13 crore shares.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An open offer at Rs 100 per share completed payment to shareholders on March 15, 2024. The acquirer then purchases shares in the open market at Rs 130 per share on August 20, 2024. Does Regulation 8(10) apply, and if so, by when must the difference be paid to shareholders who tendered in the open offer?
items.answer: 26 weeks from March 15, 2024 is approximately September 15, 2024. August 20, 2024 falls within this window, so Regulation 8(10) applies. The acquirer must pay Rs 30 per share (Rs 130 minus Rs 100) to all tendering shareholders within 60 days from August 20, 2024, i.e., by approximately October 19, 2024.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer's total consideration payable under an open offer is Rs 600 crore. Under Regulation 17(1), the required escrow is Rs 235 crore. The acquirer intends to fund the entire escrow via bank guarantee. What minimum cash amount must they additionally deposit with a scheduled commercial bank?
items.answer: At least 1% of total consideration payable = 1% of Rs 600 crore = Rs 6 crore must be deposited in cash.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer makes a mandatory open offer where the total consideration payable is Rs 400 crore. What is the non-refundable fee payable to SEBI under Regulation 16(1) at the time of filing the draft letter of offer?
items.answer: Consideration is more than Rs 10 crore but less than or equal to Rs 1,000 crore: fee = 0.5% of offer size = 0.5% × Rs 400 crore = Rs 2 crore.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: SEBI issued its comments on the draft letter of offer on April 7, 2025. Assuming no intervening non-working days, what is the last permissible date on which the tendering period can commence, and when is the last date of the tendering period?
items.answer: The tendering period must commence no later than 12 working days from April 7, 2025 = approximately April 23, 2025 (adding 12 working days). The tendering period then remains open for 10 working days, so the last date of the tendering period = approximately May 7, 2025 (adding 10 working days from April 23).

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: An acquirer holds 40% voting rights in a target company with 200 crore total shares. They wish to make a voluntary open offer under Regulation 6. What is the minimum number of shares for which the offer must be made under Regulation 7(2)?
items.answer: At least 10% additional voting rights = 10% of 200 crore total shares = 20 crore shares.

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do Regulation 3(1) and Regulation 3(5) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 contradict each other about the shareholding threshold triggering a mandatory open offer?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Do the main provision and the 2020 proviso of Regulation 3(2) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 contradict each other about the annual creep acquisition limit?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: SEBI
items.question: Is there a contradiction between Regulation 7(1) and Regulation 7(2) about the minimum open offer size under SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011?
items.answer: No

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: When did SEBI introduce separate prohibitions on wilful defaulters and fugitive economic offenders making open offers under the Takeovers Regulations, and what triggered these additions?
items.answer: The prohibition on wilful defaulters (Regulation 6A) was inserted by the Second Amendment Regulations, 2016, effective May 25, 2016, following Reserve Bank of India guidelines on wilful defaulters. The prohibition on fugitive economic offenders (Regulation 6B) was inserted by the Second Amendment Regulations, 2018, effective September 11, 2018, following the enactment of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: How was the deadline for making upward revisions to the offer price changed under Regulation 18(4) of SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011 by the 2018 amendments?
items.answer: Prior to the 2018 amendment, an acquirer could make upward revisions to the offer price up to three working days before the commencement of the tendering period. The Second Amendment Regulations, 2018 (effective September 11, 2018) reduced this window to one working day before the commencement of the tendering period, tightening the timeline for last-minute price revisions.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: When did SEBI introduce the higher 49% open offer threshold for entities listed on the Innovators Growth Platform (formerly Institutional Trading Platform), and what changes were made simultaneously?
items.answer: The Amendment Regulations, 2021, effective May 5, 2021, inserted Regulations 3(5) and 6(4) providing that the 25% mandatory open offer threshold reads as 49% for IGP-listed entities. Simultaneously, the same amendment renamed 'institutional trading platform' to 'Innovators Growth Platform' throughout the regulations.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: How did the SEBI Takeovers Regulations provisions on combined open offer and delisting evolve from 2013 to 2021?
items.answer: In 2013, a basic Regulation 5A was inserted allowing an acquirer making an open offer to also delist under the Delisting Regulations, 2009, with specific disclosure conditions. In December 2021, the Third Amendment Regulations substituted the old Regulation 5A with a comprehensive new framework referencing the updated Delisting Regulations, 2021. The new Regulation 5A introduced: (a) detailed conditions for acquirer eligibility; (b) a two-payment structure (indicative price if delisting threshold met, open offer price if not); (c) a two-attempt delisting structure; and (d) updated timelines for withdrawal announcements.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: When were housing finance companies and systemically important NBFCs added to the list of pledgees exempt from disclosure obligations under the encumbrance provisions of SEBI Takeovers Regulations, and what was the scope of the original exemption?
items.answer: The original exemption in Regulation 29(4) covered only scheduled commercial banks and public financial institutions acting as pledgees in ordinary business. The Third Amendment Regulations, 2018, effective December 31, 2018, expanded this to also include housing finance companies (registered with NHB, deposit-taking or with asset size of Rs 500 crore or more) and systemically important non-banking financial companies. The expansion recognised the growing role of these institutions as lenders against pledged shares.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What happened to the annual continual disclosure requirement for promoters and major shareholders under SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, and when was it removed?
items.answer: Regulation 30, which required every person holding 25% or more of voting rights and all promoters to disclose their aggregate shareholding as of March 31 each financial year (within 7 working days from year-end), was omitted by the Second Amendment Regulations, 2021, with effect from April 1, 2022. This was part of a broader overhaul of disclosure obligations, including changes to Regulation 29. The annual continual disclosure was likely subsumed into or replaced by disclosure requirements under the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: What significant change did the SEBI Takeovers Amendment Regulations, 2025 make to who can conduct share valuations for open offers, and what transitional protection was provided for ongoing assignments?
items.answer: The 2025 Amendment Regulations, effective January 3, 2026, replaced the requirement that valuations for infrequently traded shares (Regulation 8(2)(e) and 8(4)) and consideration shares (Regulation 9(5)) be done by the acquirer and the manager to the open offer (or an independent merchant banker/chartered accountant with 10 years' experience) with the requirement for an independent registered valuer as defined under section 247 of the Companies Act, 2013. A transition period of 9 months was provided for valuation assignments already underway before the amendment came into force.

items.sourceDetail: Securities and Exchange Board of India (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 2011
items.question: When was the regulatory sandbox exemption introduced into SEBI Takeovers Regulations 2011, and what is the maximum duration for which SEBI can grant such an exemption?
items.answer: The regulatory sandbox provision (Regulation 31A) was inserted by the SEBI (Regulatory Sandbox) (Amendment) Regulations, 2020, effective April 17, 2020. SEBI can grant exemptions from any provisions of the Takeovers Regulations for a period not exceeding 12 months, subject to such conditions as SEBI deems appropriate, to enable testing of new products, processes, services, or business models in a live environment.

items.question: What regulation number is cited regarding Allowing Offer for Sale (OFS) and Rights Entitlements (RE) transactions?
items.answer: Regulation 9

items.sourceDetail: 3.4.4.1 Registrars and Share Transfer agents shall accept partial dematerialisation | governance
